mcqs.question: A staff engineer is pairing with an engineer in their first month on the codebase. Which protocol best prevents the senior from quietly taking over?
options: Ping-pong — the senior writes a failing test, the junior makes it pass, and they alternate
Strong-style — the senior navigates and may not touch the keyboard; the junior types every line
Timer-based rotation — swap the keyboard every 15 minutes regardless of who is mid-thought
Let the senior drive first to demonstrate the codebase, then hand over
mcqs.explanation: Strong-style makes takeover structurally impossible — the person with the idea has to route it through the other person's hands, so the junior can't spectate and the senior can't grab the keyboard "just for this bit." Ping-pong splits work evenly but still lets the senior implement half of it themselves, and a plain timer or a demo-first approach relies on discipline exactly where good intentions usually fail.

mcqs.question: What does async code review provide that pairing loses entirely?
options: Detection of edge cases the author didn't consider
A second engineer who understands the change well enough to maintain it
A written, searchable record of why the change was made and what was rejected
Verification that tests actually cover the risky behavior
mcqs.explanation: A pairing session leaves no artifact — the reasoning, the alternatives and the sign-off live in two people's memories unless someone deliberately writes them up, which is a real cost when you're debugging this code in eighteen months. Edge-case detection, shared understanding and test scrutiny all happen during pairing, often more thoroughly than a diff reader manages.

mcqs.question: Which factor most distinguishes effective remote pairing from screen-sharing at someone?
options: Whether the session is recorded so the pair can review it afterwards
Whether both engineers are using the same editor and keybindings
Whether the connection has low enough latency for comfortable typing
Whether the non-driver can act — move the cursor, jump to a definition, edit — or only watch
mcqs.explanation: Agency is what turns a passive viewer into a navigator: being able to explore independently and take the keyboard is the difference between collaborating and watching a demo, which is why Live Share and Code With Me exist rather than plain screen share. Latency matters and is worth solving, but a fast one-way stream is still a one-way stream, and identical tooling is exactly what those tools remove the need for.

mcqs.question: Which of these is the weakest use of a pairing session?
options: A bug that has beaten one engineer for a full day
Adding a standard CRUD endpoint that closely mirrors four existing ones
Designing the data model for a new subsystem, with the shape still undecided
A change to the payment retry path, where a mistake double-charges customers
mcqs.explanation: Routine work that one person already knows how to do gets roughly 1.1x the throughput for 2x the engineer-hours, with almost no knowledge transfer — an async review catches what's needed. The other three are where pairing earns its cost: breaking fixation on a stuck bug, redirecting a design while a redirect still costs seconds, and getting two people who genuinely understand a high-blast-radius path.

mcqs.question: Your team lets pairs self-organize, and the two seniors consistently pair on the interesting problems while juniors work solo with async review. Why is that a problem?
options: It concentrates ownership of the interesting work, which hurts morale more than it hurts output
Two seniors will move too fast and skip tests without a third perspective
Senior-senior pairing on familiar work is the lowest-return pairing, while the highest-return pairing across the experience gap never gets scheduled
Juniors reviewing senior code asynchronously will rubber-stamp it
mcqs.explanation: Two people who already know the codebase transfer almost no knowledge, so you pay 2x for a marginal quality gain — meanwhile the pairing that would move the team most is the one comfort-based self-organization never produces. The morale effect is real but secondary, and the fix is scheduled rotation across the gap on interesting work, not adding a third person or changing who reviews whom.
